newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea risks inflation with petrol price hike.
newsitem.headline: South Korea risks inflation with petrol price hike.

text.p: South Korea delivered a year-end bombshell on Friday by raising petrol prices by 12 percent in a bid to conserve energy and help narrow the current account deficit.
Economists said the move risked fueling inflation at a time when a falling won is driving up the cost of imports.
The Ministry of Finance and Economy said it would increase domestic petrol prices by 12 percent to 815 won ($0.97) a litre from 727 won, effective on Saturday.
This is the first time petrol prices have gone over the 800 won level and was the biggest energy price hike since 1992.

At the same time, the tax on petrol transportation will rise 20 percent, to 414 won from 345 won, the ministry said. A tax on petrol used to fund education, and the value-added tax on petrol will also rise.
Extra tax revenue estimated at 754 billion won would be used to improve social infrastructure including roads, railways and a new airport, it said.
Higher taxes are expected to cut petrol consumption by about 1.55 million barrels a year, the ministry said. Consumption last year was 59.38 million barrels.
"South Korea's petrol prices are lower than that of most industrialised countries, triggering petrol overspending and traffic congestion," a ministry official said.
However, Kim Sung-shik, an economist at LG Economic Research Institute, said the move may backfire.
"It's unlikely that many people would stop driving cars because of the hike," he said.
"The expected slowdown in petrol consumption will have limited impact on the current account deficit, but the rise in petrol prices would fuel inflation next year."
South Korea's November consumer price index grew 4.3 percent from the end of 1995, slightly under the target for all this year of 4.5 percent.
Economists said the petrol price hike was likely to fuel inflation in various ways.

"The price hike would hit the transportation industry, which would want to raise fares," said Kim of LG. "The government will soon find it difficult to control other service charges, and possibly lose a grip on inflation."
Backing the inflation worries, the won has dropped 8.1 percent so far this year.
The ministry said the country's petrol consumption has risen an average of 20 percent annually between 1990 and 1995.
"This is desirable considering the need to slow South Korea's huge petrol spending," said Lee Sang-koo, an energy analyst at Hyundai Securities.
"For a country that depends entirely on crude oil imports, it seems like we're on a right track. But it's such a psychological shock for the consumers," he said.
Analysts and economists pointed out that the government saw the step as a great opportunity to slash the snowballing current account deficit.
"The government believes the slowdown in oil imports would help narrow the current account deficit next year," said Lee of Hyundai.
The central Bank of Korea says the current account deficit will reach $18 billion next year, compared with a $22 billion shortfall this year. The deficit was $8.95 billion in 1995.
(Conversion $1 = 843 won)
